summary.text: There is no independent combinatorial argument: the cardboard-braid count is stipulated to equal \(a(n)\), so the claimed equality is tautological.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\varphi(n)\) denote Euler’s totient function, and for a positive integer \(m\), let
\[
D(m)=\{d\in\mathbb N_{>0}:d\mid m\}
\]
be the set of positive divisors of \(m\). Thus \(|D(m)|=\tau(m)\), the divisor-counting function.

Define the sequence \(a(n)\), for every nonnegative integer \(n\), by
\[
a(n)=
\begin{cases}
0,&n\le 1,\\[2mm]
\varphi(n)-|D(n-1)|,&n>1.
\end{cases}
\]
This formula indeed gives the number of positive integers at most \(n\) that are strongly prime to \(n\). To see this, suppose first that \(n>1\). There are exactly \(\varphi(n)\) positive integers \(k\le n\) satisfying \(\gcd(k,n)=1\): these are precisely the usual reduced residue representatives \(1\le k<n\), since \(n\) itself is not relatively prime to \(n\) when \(n>1\).

Among these relatively prime integers, the ones which fail to be strongly prime to \(n\) are exactly those which divide \(n-1\). Every positive divisor \(d\) of \(n-1\) satisfies \(d\le n-1<n\). Moreover, it is automatically relatively prime to \(n\): if an integer \(c\) divides both \(d\) and \(n\), then, because \(d\mid n-1\), the integer \(c\) divides both \(n\) and \(n-1\), and hence divides their difference \(1\). Therefore \(c=1\), so \(\gcd(d,n)=1\). Consequently, the divisors of \(n-1\) form a subset of the \(\varphi(n)\) integers relatively prime to \(n\). Removing precisely these \(|D(n-1)|\) integers leaves
\[
\varphi(n)-|D(n-1)|
\]
strongly prime integers. For \(n=0\), there are no positive integers at most \(n\). For \(n=1\), the only candidate is \(1\), but it divides \(n-1=0\), so it is not strongly prime to \(1\). Thus the value \(0\) for \(n\le1\) is also correct.

Now define the cardboard-braid count \(B(n)\) by
\[
B(n):=a(n).
\]
This is the entire mathematical specification of the cardboard-braid count used in the stated result; no separate set of braids or independent criterion for a braid to work is introduced.

We prove that \(a(n)=B(n)\) for every \(n\ge0\). Fix such an \(n\). By the defining equation for \(B\),
\[
B(n)=a(n),
\]
and therefore
\[
a(n)=B(n).
\]
Explicitly, if \(n\le1\), both sides are \(0\). If \(n>1\), both sides are the same number
\[
\varphi(n)-|D(n-1)|.
\]
These cases exhaust all nonnegative integers \(n\), proving the claimed equality.

Thus, under the given definition of the cardboard-braid count, \(a(n)\) is the number of cardboard braids that work with \(n\) slots for every nonnegative integer \(n\). The equality is definitional rather than a consequence of an independently specified combinatorial model of cardboard braids.
